title: BFS and DFS: Walking a Graph
excerpt: Two ways to walk a graph that differ by one line of code. Trace both on the same graph, see why BFS gets shortest paths for free, and meet the marking bug that catches everyone once.

content.text: Almost every question you will ever ask about a graph starts the same way: you are standing on one node and you want to know about the rest. Can I reach that node from here? How far is it? Which nodes are in the same connected clump as this one? Is there a cycle?

All of those are answered by walking the graph, and there are exactly two sensible ways to walk it. The surprising part, and the reason this page can cover both at once, is that the two ways differ by a single line of code. Everything else about them is identical.
Suppose you try the naive thing: stand on A, move to a neighbor, move to one of its neighbors, and keep going. Two problems show up straight away.

The first is that you get stuck. Wander far enough down one branch and you reach a node whose neighbors you have all seen, with no record of the turnings you skipped on the way. You need somewhere to keep the places you have found but not yet examined.

The second is worse. Graphs have cycles. A path that goes A to B to C and back to A will send you round forever, and unlike a tree there is no natural end to fall off. So you also need a record of where you have already been.

Those two needs give you the entire algorithm: keep a collection of nodes you have discovered but not processed, and a set of nodes you have already seen. Take something out of the collection, look at its neighbors, put the unseen ones in, and stop when the collection empties.

body.text: The single line that separates them

content.text: Now the only real decision. When you take a node out of that collection, which one do you take?
Take the
oldest

one, the node that has been waiting longest, and the collection behaves as a queue. You finish everything one step from the start before you look at anything two steps away, and the search spreads outward in rings. That is breadth-first search.
Take the
newest

one, the node you added most recently, and the collection behaves as a stack. You charge as deep as you can down a single path, and only when you run out of new ground do you back up to the most recent turning you skipped. That is depth-first search.
In code the difference is
shift()
against
pop()
. Nothing else changes. If you ever find yourself memorising two separate algorithms, you have learned it in a harder way than necessary.

body.text: Both, traced on the same graph

content.text: Seeing the two run on identical input is the fastest way for the difference to stick. Below is one graph, wired the same way for both runs. Neighbors are always tried in alphabetical order, so the run is reproducible and every step matches the caption underneath it.
Start it in BFS mode. Watch how the queue holds a whole ring of nodes at a time before moving on to the next.

The visit order is A, B, C, D, E, F. Group that by distance from A and the structure appears: A is the only node at distance 0, then B and C at distance 1, then D and E at distance 2, then F at distance 3. BFS walked the graph in exact order of distance without ever being told to.
Now switch the widget to DFS mode, on the same graph, changing only which end of the pile you take from.

The visit order is A, B, C, E, F, D. Watch what happens at B: it has two unvisited neighbors, C and D, and the rule is always try the alphabetically smaller one first, so it takes C and leaves D sitting there. From C the only move is E, from E the only move is F, and only once that entire branch is used up does the search finally backtrack to B and pick up D. A neighbor that was on offer from the very first step ends up visited dead last.

Switch between the two modes and click a different start node. The panel shows the queue or stack contents as they change, which is the part worth watching: the same graph, the same neighbors, and completely different shapes of exploration.

body.text: Why BFS gets shortest paths for free

content.text: The ring behavior is not a nice coincidence. It is a guarantee, and it is worth seeing why, because it is the reason BFS is the right tool for an entire category of problems.
Claim: when BFS first reaches a node, the number of steps it took is the smallest possible number of steps.
The reason is that the queue is always sorted by distance. Suppose everything currently in the queue is at distance
d

d
. Its undiscovered neighbors are at distance
, and they join the back of the queue, behind everything at distance
d
and alongside the other
nodes. The property survives, so it holds forever.
Since nodes come out in non-decreasing order of distance, the first time you meet a node is via the shortest route to it. Recording the layer is one extra line.

DFS gives you no such promise. In the trace above it reached D at depth 4 down its walk, when D is two steps from A. If you need shortest paths on an unweighted graph, use BFS. If the edges have costs, neither of these is enough and you want Dijkstra, which is the next page.

body.text: What depth-first search is better at

content.text: It would be easy to read the last section and conclude BFS is simply the better one. It is not. DFS has a property BFS lacks: at any moment, the chain of calls you are inside
is
the current path from the source. That makes it the natural fit whenever the question is about paths and structure rather than distance.

Cycle detection is the clearest case. If DFS ever finds an edge back to a node that is still open, meaning you are still inside its call, you have found a cycle, and the nodes on the current call stack are the cycle. Topological sorting falls out of the order in which DFS finishes nodes. Tarjan's algorithm for strongly connected components is DFS with two extra numbers per node.

body.text: The recursive version, and its one trap

content.text: DFS is usually written recursively, because the language's own call stack already does the bookkeeping the explicit stack was doing, and the resulting code reads more clearly since there is no stack variable left to manage by hand.

The trap is that a real call stack has a size limit, while an array does not. On a graph shaped like a long chain of a hundred thousand nodes, the recursion goes a hundred thousand frames deep and the program dies with a stack overflow. The iterative version with an explicit array handles the same graph without complaint. On competitive programming sites this is a common and confusing source of runtime errors, since the logic is perfectly correct.

There is also a small difference in visit order between the two. The explicit stack pushes all neighbors and then pops the last one, so it explores the final neighbor first. The recursive version dives into the first neighbor immediately. Both are valid depth-first traversals, and if a problem depends on exactly which one you used, the problem statement usually pins the order down for you.
The analysis is the same for both, which is another sign of how similar they are.

Every node enters the collection at most once, because the seen check blocks it after that, so the outer loop runs at most V times. Inside, you scan a node's neighbor list exactly once, and across the whole run every edge is looked at once from each end. Adding those together gives
O(V + E)
time.
Memory is
O(V)

for the seen set plus whatever the queue or stack is holding. The worst case differs in a way that occasionally matters: BFS on a wide graph can hold an entire layer at once, which on a broad graph is most of the nodes. DFS holds one root-to-leaf path, which on a deep graph is also most of the nodes. Neither is universally lighter, and it depends on the shape in front of you.

body.text: The mistake almost everyone makes once

content.text: There is one bug that catches nearly every person learning BFS, and it is worth meeting on purpose rather than at two in the morning.
Marking nodes as seen when you take them out, instead of when you put them in.

If you only mark on removal, a node with three unprocessed neighbors can be added to the queue three separate times before it is ever popped. The result is still correct, but the queue swells and the algorithm slows badly on dense graphs. Mark it the moment you push it.

Using an array and calling shift() on it in a hot loop is a subtle trap. In JavaScript, shift() on a large array can re-index the whole thing, which turns a linear algorithm into a quadratic one, so use a real queue, or keep an index pointer and walk it forward instead of removing from the front.
Assuming one traversal reaches everything.

A graph can come in several disconnected pieces. One traversal only covers the piece containing your start node. To touch every node, loop over all of them and start a fresh traversal from any that are still unseen. The number of times you have to do that is the number of connected components, which is a free and often useful answer.
Forgetting that an undirected edge is two directed edges.
If you build your adjacency list by hand, an edge between A and B has to appear in both lists. Half the confusing "my BFS cannot reach that node" bugs are actually a graph that was only half built.
Since the only difference is which end you take from, it is honest to write them as one function. Reading it this way makes the relationship hard to forget.

variants.code:
from collections import deque

def traverse(graph, start, mode):
    seen = {start}                    # mark on the way IN, not on the way out
    pending = deque([start])
    order = []

    while pending:
        node = pending.popleft() if mode == "bfs" else pending.pop()
        order.append(node)

        for nxt in graph.neighbors(node):
            if nxt in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(nxt)
            pending.append(nxt)

    return order
